pr.title: gh-142830: prevent some crashes when mutating `sqlite3` callbacks
pr.body:
This is _not_ a complete fix because there are other callbacks that need to be tested. I could technically split the PR into two but I preferred testing the conversion to `PyObject *` in the same PR.

<!-- gh-issue-number: gh-142830 -->
* Issue: gh-142830
<!-- /gh-issue-number -->

+class AuthorizerTests(MemoryDatabaseMixin, unittest.TestCase):

+    def assert_not_authorized(self, func, /, *args, **kwargs):

+    # Tests for checking that callback context mutations do not crash.
+    # Regression tests for https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/142830.

@@ -0,0 +1,2 @@
+:mod:`sqlite3`: fix use-after-free crashes when the connection's callbacks
+are mutated during a callback execution. Patch by Bénédikt Tran.

I think I will add some macros or functions for holding the refs when needed.

So I've tried, but I miserably failed. Each callback creates a shared callback context that is either freed when the connection dies or when it got replaced. The problem is when I replace a callback:

- Define cb(). This creates some conn->ctx.
- Execute cb. During the execution, remove cb.
- Removal of cb triggers removal of conn->ctx (it gets replaced by NULL) and conn->ctx is freed directly (deferring freeing the memory isn't possible because no one is tracking it after it's replaced in the connection's object)

Maybe I got it wrong or understood the mechanism wrongly, but relying on the GC is much more easier.

When the callback is added, set its refcount to 1. If it is replaced, decrement its refcount. When the callback is called, increment its refcount (so that it doesn't disappear from under our feet), after calling it, decrement its refcount. If after any decrement it becomes 0, free it. This is very similar to how refcounts work for PyObject, but We don't need PyTypeObject and other boilerplate.

Other way is just make local strong references to `callback` and `module` (if needed) and a weak reference to state (if needed) for the time of calling the callback, On this way you will only need to change the code that calls the callback, and use Python refcounts.

Ok I'll see what I can with that but to be sure, there is no "finalization" callback that is called after the callback is called, that is:

> after calling it, decrement its refcount

This means, decrementing the refcount of the context object that was passed to the callback itself, right?

> When the callback is added, set its refcount to 1

Actually the reason my code crashed was because I put it at 0... But I'll add the rest as you told me. Thanks!

> This means, decrementing the refcount of the context object that was passed to the callback itself, right?

Yes. you manage the refcount of the context struct in the same way as you currently manage the refcount of the context Python object.

In other approach, you can manage the refcounts of `callback` and other context attributes.
I do not talk what you should do, I only describe variants which may be more laconic than the current PR.

I actually tried this initial approach but I thought "why not just rely on the GC" and then went with a full-fledged PyObject. Using a PyObject definitely makes my life easier as it's not me who's responsible for that but it's also fine to use another strategy that doesn't need this overhead (considering _every_ statement would require INCREF/DECREF of the entire context, it's clearly not a good idea indeed).

@serhiy-storchaka Thanks for the guidance! it's a bit annoying to do the manual refcounting and someone could easily forget to do it, but it's definitely better for the diff. I can also backport this PR with more confidence.

issue_comments.body: Earlier we relied on GC for these callbacks; IOW, we did not use the SQLite C API provided destructor machinery. Perhaps we should revert to that again. It is more verbose, but it's less hacky than what the current solution has grown to be.
